title: Class templates
learningGoals: make objects with a type in angle brackets

youtube.title: C++ Class Templates: Build Your Own Container | C++ Programming EP 70
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a class template, make objects with a type in angle brackets and build a small stack, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Class templates · 0:52 A Box template · 1:32 One template, two classes · 2:02 Second program · 3:02 Recap · 3:32 Bug of the Day · 4:20 Challenge · 4:40 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "BOX<T>" in tomato on lilac; Xecxec next to a labelled box that can hold anything; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a labelled box that can hold anything

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we build a container. With a class template, the same class can hold ints, doubles or strings.

scenes.onScreen: "Class templates": numbered lines (1. A class template has a type placeholder; 2. You name the type when you make an object; 3. Each type gets its own class) and an analogy card: a storage box with a blank label: write int, double or string on it
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A class template puts a type placeholder on the whole class. When you make an object, you name the type in angle brackets. The compiler then builds a class for that type. The standard library containers, such as vector, are class templates. Think of a storage box with a blank label. You write int, double or string on it when you use it.
points: A class template has a type placeholder
You name the type when you make an object
Each type gets its own class

analogy.title: Class templates
analogy.body: A storage box with a blank label: write int, double or string on it

scenes.onScreen: box.cpp: a Box holds one value of any type
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] T is the placeholder. [HL 7] The member has type T. [HL 10] The constructor takes a T. [HL 11] The getter returns a T. [HL 15] Here T is int. [HL 16] Here T is string. They are two different classes. The output is seven, and Goa.

scenes.onScreen: a table of the classes that the compiler builds
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Each use of the template with a new type makes a new class. Box of int holds an int. Box of string holds a string. They do not share anything, except the recipe.

diagram.caption: a table of the classes that the compiler builds

scenes.onScreen: stack.cpp: a Stack template built on a vector
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 7] Inside, a vector of T holds the items. [HL 10] Push adds an item at the end. [HL 11] Pop removes the last item, and returns it. [HL 20] Here we make a stack of ints. [HL 21] We push one, two and three. [HL 25] Pop gives the last item first. The output is three, two, one.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as stack dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints three, two and one.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A class template has a type placeholder. Two. Name the type in angle brackets when you make an object. Three. Each type gets its own class. Four. Library containers are class templates. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A class template has a type placeholder.
Name the type in angle brackets when you make an object.
Each type gets its own class.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A missing template argument
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We make a Box with no type. The compiler says class template argument deduction failed. It has nothing to learn T from. Write the type in angle brackets, as in Box of int.

scenes.onScreen: My template is an open-minded class. It accepts any type, but it still wants a label.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: My template is an open-minded class. It accepts any type, but it still wants a label.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: make a Pair template
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a class template Pair with two members of the same type T. Add a function that returns the bigger one. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: pair and tuple. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

box.cpp: In function 'int main()':
box.cpp:11:9: error: class template argument deduction failed:
   11 |     Box b;
      |         ^
bug.why: The compiler cannot guess T when there is no constructor argument to learn it from. Write the type in angle brackets.

pun: "My template is an open-minded class. It accepts any type, but it still wants a label."
challenge: Write a class template Pair with two members of the same type T. Add a function that returns the bigger one.
challengeAnswer: Store two T members. In the function, return the first if it is bigger than the second, otherwise the second.
